speaker: John
line: In a hypothetical course called Efficient Transformer Architectures, today’s lecture is on Learnable Subspace Projections for Large Language Model Compression. As models grow, researchers are looking for ways to reduce their memory and compute demands. Work such as Swift-S-V-D studies low-rank compression, while x K-V addresses a related memory bottleneck in attention caches. This paper asks whether compression should follow a layer’s statistics or the model’s output. Yes, Noah?

speaker: Noah
line: Hi, Professor. Why might a direction that looks unimportant in one layer matter to the whole model?

speaker: John
line: Because a layer’s local statistics do not necessarily reveal how its changes affect later computations. Imagine removing a quiet instrument from an orchestra: it may be faint on its own, but still matter to the final sound. The authors’ motivation is that energy or reconstruction error alone can miss a direction’s downstream importance. Their method, L-S-P, learns which directions to remove by comparing the compressed model’s output with the dense model’s output.

speaker: Noah
line: So L-S-P changes which directions are removed, rather than simply choosing a smaller rank?

speaker: John
line: That is the key distinction. A projector removes selected input directions from a linear layer, limiting the layer’s rank. Some layers read the same activations, so they can share a projector; for example, query, key, and value projections can be tied. Other layers are projected on their smaller side. This gives the method a way to coordinate compatible layers while still choosing different compression decisions across the network.

speaker: Noah
line: How does it decide which directions to test and how much rank to keep?

speaker: John
line: It begins with calibration activations and uses a whitened S-V-D truncation to initialize candidate projectors. Then it measures the output K-L cost of removing directions from one unit at a time, while the rest of the network remains dense. Those measurements guide a greedy rank allocation, trading output cost against parameters saved. It is a practical surrogate, not a globally optimal allocation: interactions between units are not fully captured by these isolated measurements.

speaker: Noah
line: Does training then change the original model weights as well as the projectors?

speaker: John
line: In the default setup, the pretrained weights stay frozen while the projectors are trained jointly to match the dense model’s output distribution. The paper also considers using the original task loss, but output distillation is the central approach. Once training is complete, each projection can be merged into ordinary low-rank factors. With a shared input factor, tied key and value layers can also use one narrow latent representation.

speaker: John
line: The cleanest test of whether learning matters is the No L-S-P control. It shares L-S-P’s initialization, allocated ranks, and ties, but leaves the projectors untrained. On Llama two seven B at 70% compression, WikiText-2 test perplexity is 10.9 for trained L-S-P and 222.8 for No L-S-P; lower perplexity means better next-token prediction. S-V-D L-L-M, the strongest baseline in that setting, scores 13.3.

speaker: Noah
line: Is that perplexity result directly comparable to the zero-shot accuracy result?

speaker: John
line: They answer different questions under different protocols. For perplexity, calibration uses 1,024 sequences of 2,048 tokens from the WikiText-2 training split. Separately, the Alpaca-calibrated zero-shot evaluation reports a 42.2% mean plain accuracy for L-S-P, versus 36% for S-V-D L-L-M. That mean is the arithmetic average across ARC-easy, PIQA, OpenBookQA, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, and MathQA, not a measure of every capability.

speaker: John
line: There are also deployment results, but it is important to keep throughput and memory capacity distinct. At 70% compression, batch size 1, and a 512-token context, measured decoding reaches 221 tokens per second for L-S-P versus 141 for the dense model. A separate latent-cache calculation gives 38.9 gibibytes for weights plus cache at 128,000 cached tokens and batch size 8, versus 524.6 gibibytes dense. That capacity result requires attention software that stores the shared narrow latent.

speaker: Noah
line: Could the latent cache itself explain the measured decoding speedup?

speaker: John
line: Not from these results. The speed measurement uses a short context and a full-width K-V cache; the latent-cache figure concerns memory capacity under a different setup. Compression also has costs: measuring K-L and training projectors take resources. At a fixed compression ratio, factorized methods can have similar operation counts, so actual speed depends on the shape and number of matrix multiplies and the inference conditions, not just the parameter reduction.

speaker: John
line: Compared with S-V-D L-L-M, L-S-P replaces a closed-form, layer-wise reconstruction choice with projectors trained against a network-level output objective, while freezing the pretrained weights. Dobi-S-V-D is another useful contrast: it optimizes truncation positions, but its basis is still closed-form. This distinction is not simply whether a method uses a loss; it is whether the removed subspaces themselves are learned end to end against the model’s output.

speaker: Noah
line: Does the evidence show that L-S-P preserves behavior broadly across tasks and users?

speaker: John
line: No. The reported evidence supports an advantage in the specified WikiText-2 and six-benchmark conditions, not universal behavior preservation. The authors also caution that aggregate results can hide uneven losses on underrepresented populations, domains, or rare behaviors. The broader implication is a shift in what compression can optimize: instead of treating a layer’s spectrum as the final guide, researchers can use model outputs to inform which directions are expendable, while still accounting for calibration and allocation limits.

speaker: John
line: The takeaway is that compression is a choice of directions, not merely a choice of rank. L-S-P shows why learning removals against network output can be a more informative guide than relying on a layer’s spectrum alone, though its evidence remains bounded by its calibration data and approximate rank allocator.
